name: Question 12
problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/62c8f6d7db345ce76bd164bb52c13e5edef9c04f18f4f07501c8694e7f64b554.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $x={e}^{y}$ from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{2}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={e}^{t}\,y=t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/ba6285008fd90835fdbf73203b76a0a01d713889d9939979aaec54bebd0a8c49.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}={t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x}={e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2})\cdot (1)-({e}^{-t})\cdot ({e}^{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of F across C measured with respect to a unit normal vector n on C is given by ∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx. To apply this formula,

  • the curve should be parameterized as r(t) for t∈[a,b], and

  • the unit normal vector n must be a 90∘ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector T(t).

Parameterizing the curve C, we have x=ety=t,t∈[0,1].

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point (1,0) to the point (e,1). Therefore, n is indeed a 90∘ clockwise rotation of T, so we can apply the above formula for the flux.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=y2=t2,Q(x,y)=1x=e−t.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(et)=et,dydt=ddt(t)=1.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx=∫01(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫01(t2)⋅(1)−(e−t)⋅(et)dt=∫01t2−1dt=(t33−t)|01=(13−1)−0=−23
